The recently proposed Legendre Memory Module (LMM) commended a 95% compression ratio and demonstrated superior performance on the MNIST dataset, with the ability to resume training from its compressed state. This paper introduces an enhanced version of the LMM called Empirical Legendre Memory Module (eLMM), which replaces the synthetic gradients with real gradient values obtained through parallelized training. Additionally, the eLMM model compresses the network into a single vector, achieving a 95% compression ratio identical to the original LMM. Furthermore, the eLMM model surpasses the state-of-the-art MNIST test accuracy of 97.41%, offering a 71% reduction in parameters and a 93% decrease in trainable parameters compared to the original LMM model. This paper also showcases the eLMM's versatility by applying it to more challenging datasets, including CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100.

As we pursue the quest for new physics, particularly beyond the Standard Model, 
a compelling argument exists to suspect the presence of additional, lightly 
interacting entities beyond the reach of conventional detection methods. 
To guide the exploration of new interactions and particles, this article presents 
an overview of the challenges involved in detecting particles with minimal 
interactions, along with the potential these new particles hold for advancing 
our understanding of the fundamental nature of the universe.

In a labeling game with evolving rules, new players not only execute but also adjust these rules, which involves assigning meanings to established terms. This study focuses on how participant turnover affects the meanings of words, where every time step introduces a new participant with their own set of word assignments. It is demonstrated that under specific conditions, the average distance between assigned terms and their corresponding ideal values converges to zero. Specifically, for any given precision epsilon, it becomes likely that a random participant's word assignments align with their respective references within a specified time frame that depends on the total number of participants, the labeling efficiency, and the precision level. Additionally, it was found that the rate of convergence or the time required to achieve consensus varies according to a specific formula, which depends on the efficiency of the labeling process and the rate at which old participants depart and new ones arrive. By manipulating a simulated economy, it was observed that the average exchange rates calculated by participants do indeed converge to their corresponding true values. This convergence was also visually confirmed through a three-dimensional plot showing the distorting effect of participant turnover on assignments, which diminishes as the efficiency of the labeling process increases.

Momentum-based methods in physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) can effectively mitigate spectral bias by incorporating past gradients of the loss function into parameter updates, in contrast to conventional stochastic gradient descent which tends to favor lower-frequency solutions. The introduction of momentum in PINNs leads to a significant reduction in spectral bias, as evidenced by the increased performance of the model across various frequency ranges. The use of momentum in PINNs also improves their capacity to handle complex problems and enhances their training efficiency by promoting convergence. The improved performance of momentum-based PINNs is attributed to the regularized effect of past gradients which, together with parameter updates, facilitates PINN training and generalization. Theoretical analysis reveals that momentum-based PINNs regularize the neural network using a combination of the Hessian and gradient norms, while the adjoint method in PINNs can be interpreted as a method of parameter regularization through the adjoint variable derived from the optimality conditions of the loss function.

In the context of hyperbolic partial differential equations, we examine the exponential stability of a specific wave system with connections, originating in the Kelvin-Voigt damping model, but with the damping term altered locally to expedite analysis. By employing compactness-based techniques and a resolvent estimate in the spectral theory of elliptic operators, we demonstrate the existence of a stable resolvent and a Hille-Phillips compact vector-valued function associated with the modified damping system. Consequently, we derive the associated evolution equation's well-posedness with exponential stability, focusing particularly on the influence of the damping's limited spectrum and connections. This analysis yields acute insights into the localized damping's behavior within connected systems.

Our proposed approach to reinforcement learning involves a two-part framework consisting of a Model-driven learner utilizing Inductive Logic Programming and an layer of Hierarchical learners. We aim to facilitate the acquisition of a knowledge base regarding the decision-making policies and strategies utilized by an optimal agent. This knowledge base can then be leveraged to enhance the transparency and understanding of the agent's cognitive processes. We have demonstrated through theoretical analysis and experimental evaluation that our proposed methodology yields a transparent agent aligned with the policies and strategies identified by the knowledge base. Furthermore, the introduction of a hierarchical structure of learners enables the agent to attain more efficient training. We have tested and validated our methodology through the agent's successful acquisition of a subspecies of a difficult, non-trivial decision-making task.

We investigate how the vacuum in a specific input mode of a lossy bosonic interferometer becomes quantum entangled with another unmeasured mode. This interferometer system incorporates a particular $SU(1,1)$ gate, which is analogous to the $W$ gate, to generate the entanglement. By defining an effective mean field operator within the rotating wave approximation, we explore the quantum effect that emerges due to the $W$ gate's presence. This quantum effect, akin to a gravitational force, can be detected as an optical asymmetry within the interferometer by comparing the probabilities of input signals and anti-signal states. Additionally, we define an effective density matrix to represent the combined state of the two modes and utilize it to calculate the asymptotic average and standard deviation of photon numbers. Importantly, we find that the photon number distribution in one mode can be negative, indicating non-classical behavior that is a hallmark of quantum effects. To implement our proposal, we suggest using a twin-beam source with feedback paths to modulate an input field via Kerr media, enabling the simulation of the quantum compression phenomenon.

This document addresses two types of zero sum minimax problems as proposed by Fenton. The first involves finding the minimum distance between a given smooth curve and a set of lattice points within a fundamental region. The second scenario involves counting the number of sign changes in a specific type of function that involves total translates of functions at integer points within a fundamental region. By applying Fourier expansion and analyzing the zero sets of key components, we establish a link between the monotonicity of a specific weight function and the existence of solutions for the second minimax problem. Additionally, we identify several categories of curves that can be efficiently approximated by lattice points. Our approach involves a combination of elementary methods and Minkowski's Theorem.

The study of lithium isotopes, particularly $^{6}$Lithium, is gaining momentum as a potential tool in dark matter research. By utilizing lithium to create an energy-rich target, researchers can explore dark matter interactions sensitive to spin. Recent advancements in nuclear physics have uncovered higher-energy states of $^{6}$Lithium that are highly amenable to such interactions. Our analysis focuses on the novel physics that can be uncovered through investigations of $^{6}$Lithium's excited states, specifically focusing on the 1.856 MeV state accessible with relatively low-energy beams. By examining the various theoretical models that apply to both ordinary and exotic particles, we identify which dark matter interactions corresponding to that spin-sensitive state that are particularly feasible to investigate. Our investigation is further supplemented by a detailed examination of the experimental challenges posed by the latest $^{6}$Lithium measurements, as well as by the potential for future experiments using the same isotopes to a significantly higher degree of precision.

Blind image restoration, encompassing tasks like deblurring, de-noising, and
  de-shading, is a deep learning challenge. The problem's solution is complicated
  by the absence of a clear objective function and the inherent ill-positivity in the
  estimated image. The key constraint in these problems is the blind kernel, the
  unknown kernel that affects the image, along with an assumed kernel form. 
  Current methods primarily focus on eliminating noise and are not adaptable to a
  variety of kernel types. They also lack a strict mathematical guarantee for image
  quality restoration. In this context, we introduce the Kernel Mixture Model (KMM),
  a novel probabilistic framework that treats the blind kernel as a mixture of a few
  specific kernels. The KMM framework allows us to approximate the unknown kernel and
  evaluate its mathematical relationship with the image data, thereby formulating
  an objective function for the restoration task. As a proof-of-concept, we
  successfully utilize KMM for the deblurring task and achieve a superior performance
  compared to the current state-of-the-art method. The KMM code will be publicly
  available on our website.

The one-form associative Yang-Baxter equation is introduced, which encompasses uniform and non-uniform forms. By constraining the coefficients of the two-form associative Yang-Baxter equation, a consistent one-form equation is derived. It is notable that the consistent one-form equation can be viewed as a reduced version of the two-form equation. Moreover, from the point of view of bialgebras, the relationship between the two-form and one-form associative Yang-Baxter equations is explored.

Hoare logic offers a well-established strategy for formally proving the correctness of software based on its source code and specifications. Nevertheless, formally verifying programs with today's automated reasoning techniques becomes impractical due to the complexity of transforming natural language requirements into formal specifications. This paper proposes a novel approach called Natural Hoare Reasoning, where we aim to prove a filter-like program correct using natural language predicates for input requirements and no additional domain-theoretic considerations are necessary. Though fully automated methods are sought after, human intervention is still required to verify the given examples.

Distributed consensus is a foundational component of modern distributed systems, with extensive applications across various domains, including distributed databases, blockchains, and distributed ledgers.  The consensus process involves a group of entities, known as participants, working towards reaching agreement on a specific topic or value.  The value in question can be an actual data element, as seen in databases, or a virtual one, as seen in blockchain-based systems, where it refers to a specific set of transactions.

In general, consensus processes involve a leader entity that creates and disseminates proposed values, referred to as 'values,' to other participating entities, known as 'followers.'  The followers then use local information to determine whether a proposal is legitimate and, if so, they update their understanding of the proposed value accordingly.

In this study, the researchers addressed the challenge of enhancing the robustness of Canopus, a specific type of consensus process, by examining various failure scenarios and participant behaviors.  Canopus is distinct due to its ability to efficiently manage diverse value sets through the use of graphs that represent value relationships.  The participants in a Canopus consensus process typically rely on local information to assess proposal legitimacy and, if a proposal is deemed unreliable, they will inform other participants about specific failure events.

To investigate how a specific type of lipid molecule (sphingolipid) affects the overall flexibility of cell membrane membranes, which contain cholesterol, we utilized molecular dynamics simulations. Our primary concern was understanding how the presence of this lipid impacts the membrane's ability to bend. To this end, we conducted multiple simulations involving model systems consisting of various levels of cholesterol that interact with the present lipid, such as the lipid itself when it binds to other lipids. Our analysis revealed a notable correlation between the types of lipid molecules and the rate at which the membrane turns "inside out". Additionally, we observed a direct link between the types of lipid molecules and the strength of the binding between the lipids and cholesterol. Our findings also show that the measured properties are an accurate reflection of the actual behavior of the membrane. Our study further explores how the types of lipid molecules affect the organization and composition of the membrane. Our results provide valuable insights into how the types of lipid molecules impact the binding organization of the membrane.

Traditional approaches to converting a metric to a Loop quantum gravity configuration space picture often rely on specific quantum algebra representations. However, such representations come with inherent loop states, which are usually assigned a role in the theory's cosmological context. This paper explores an alternative method for deriving Loop quantum gravity models that utilizes the ADM Hamiltonian directly, resulting in a successful implementation within the context of the Hamiltonian's simple scalar field modification.

Between 2004 and 2020, researchers recorded 20 signals strong enough to exceed 100 EeV, as well as 84 signals slightly weaker but still measured to be in the range of 40 to 80 EeV, using the Pierre Auger Observatory's surface detector array located near Malvinas Altas. An investigation of the arrival directions of these extensive air showers showed no anomalies in their distribution across the horizon or seasonality. An analysis of Auger's data from 2004 to 2018 found no correlation with any specific source of ultra-high energy particles, despite being close to several major airports and airfields. Furthermore, researchers concluded that extreme cosmic rays arriving at Earth must be essentially isotropic in nature.

Incorporating deep neural networks into high-risk systems necessitates pinpointing their inherent uncertainties. This research delves into uncertainty estimation for object detection tasks via convolutional neural networks. A substantial issue with uncertainty quantification lies in self-supervising methods lacking real objective criteria. To mitigate this shortcoming, our proposed framework BayesOD self-supervises by matching the output probability distribution of a network with an expected probability distribution established upon ground-truth annotations. The framework is extensive, encompassing various distribution models such as Gaussian, Negative-Binomial, and Dirichlet-Exponential. BayesOD is versatile and can be easily integrated into existing object detection systems without modification. Performance evaluations using three image datasets reveal BayesOD surpasses state-of-the-art uncertainty assessment methods for object detection. Datasets utilized comprise VOC2007, MS-COCO (Seasons), and DetecNet. Results demonstrate BayesOD outperforms previous uncertainty estimation methods. A comparative assessment of uncertainty estimation methods is presented. Uncertainty assessment methods tested comprise CE-Gaussian, CE-Bernoulli, AE-Gaussian, AE-Bernoulli, AE-Binomial, AE-Exp, AE-Expo, AE-Dirichlet, AE-DE, AE-DE-R, Refined-Gaussian, Refined-Binomial, Refined-Bernoulli, Refined-Exp, Refined-Expo, Refined-Dirichlet, Refined-DE,

Recent interest in traffic forecasting has centered on making precise predictions for future large-scale traffic patterns, yet understanding the intricate dynamics of traffic in localized settings remains overlooked. To address this gap, this work introduces a novel approach to forecasting traffic conditions within small spatial and temporal frameworks. By utilizing a multi-modal CNN architecture, this method processes and analyzes data from urban sensors, enabling accurate predictions of future traffic patterns in detailed settings. Furthermore, a novel loss function has been introduced that minimizes the disparity between actual and predicted data within specific temporal and spatial contexts. Evaluations on two real-world datasets have demonstrated the efficacy of the proposed approach, leading to lower average prediction errors compared to existing state-of-the-art methods.

In the context of Gray categories, coherence can be achieved by adapting and integrating general coherence techniques. A significant finding suggests that the process of adapting to coherence has a universal significance, comparable to the next type in a hierarchy of categories. Furthermore, the study discovers and analyzes a crucial category of gray categories known as digray categories. Importantly, the research demonstrates that the category of gray categories includes digrays is coherent, serving as a broad and natural platform for various gray categories, including $2$-categories, monoidal categories, traced categories, and star categories. The research develops and discusses potential extensions to these findings, also outlining implications and future research possibilities arising from the study.

To ensure the optimal execution of hippocampus segmentation on convolutional neural networks (CNN), a thorough evaluation of various CNN architectures and configuration settings is required. In this research, we examine how three fundamental hippocampal portions (body, head, and tail) can be segmented utilizing seven adaptable CNNs, all trained on the same dataset of hippocampal slices. The Hippocampal segmentation in T2-weighted MRI (HipT2wMRI) dataset, comprising 375 hippocampi in training and 100 in testing phases, was utilized to train and evaluate the performance of the seizable hippocampi. The hipSeg evaluation measure was applied to assess segmentation accuracy. The outcomes reveal that incorporating HipT2wMRI data augmentation, a binary cross-entropic loss, a multi-portion discriminator, and the tail of the tail Autoencoder (tail2ae) network significantly enhances the segmentation precision of the primary hippocampal portion and the other two portions, respectively. Notably, the seizable hippocampi classifier exhibited an increased precision in the presence of hippocampal segmentation errors. Based on the experimental findings, a HipT2wMRI seizable hippocampi analysis pipeline is proposed, including hippocampus segmentation and classification, to be used in the assessment of seizure-free and hippocampal atrophy prediction in temporal lobe epilepsy patients. The study's outcomes may also be used to analyze hippocampal changes in Alzheimer's disease and other hippocampal disorders.

In coupled oscillator systems, "the pigeonhole principle" can limit certain phenomena. When two groups of oscillators with similar frequencies interact, each group's mode structure remains intact, and new, hybrid frequencies emerge only when the mode structures differ. If two groups have matching mode structures, they will not generate new hybrid frequencies. Researchers have shown that two groups of 18 and 21 oscillators, respectively, can couple without producing new frequencies, as their mode structures pivot at specific points. However, a study found that when these oscillators couple beyond these points, new frequency patterns emerge. In contrast, similar coupling in groups of 20 and 22 oscillators produces new hybrid frequencies at all stages.

The Cosmic Ray Albedo Neutron Decay (CRAND) process produces neutrons in the Earth's atmosphere that become trapped and eventually decay into protons. However, the traditional models used to estimate CRAND neutrons do not currently account for the polarization of the neutron beam, the effects of atmospheric depth, and the capture of neutrons at low Earth orbit by the proton captured neutrons (PCN). Our research utilizes Geant4 Monte Carlo tool to simulate CRAND protons and PCNs in the Earth's magnetic field, and investigates the effects of atmospheric depth, neutron polarization, and the capture of neutrons at low Earth orbit by the proton captured neutrons (PCN). The Geant4 tool has shown that the estimated number of protons from CRAND neutrons increases significantly, especially at low Earth orbit by the proton captured neutrons (PCN). Our research estimates that the observed increase in protons at low Earth orbit could be as high as 3 orders of magnitude due to the captured neutrons (PCN). In recent years, Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) have made remarkable breakthroughs in various applications, yet their performance is still not on par with traditional deep learning models for some tasks. Moreover, the lack of a unified design theory and innovative mechanisms has hindered the further advancement of GNNs. To address this challenge, this paper proposes a pioneering GNN framework called Universal Pyramid-like Shrinkage Skeleton (UPSS), which tackles two critical challenges in GNN design: multi-scale feature extraction and local structure propagation. The proposed framework comprises three modules: a hierarchical shrinkage skeleton, and dynamic link rewiring for improving information exchange between different layers. The UPSS framework outperforms previous models in various benchmarks, achieving a 10% improvement in classification accuracy. Furthermore, it sets a new benchmark in visual domain tasks, such as image classification and edge detection, by a substantial margin (5-10%) and reduces model parameters by 60%. The proposed mechanism is also applied to the existing models, leading to notable enhancements, such as a 3% increase in classification accuracy for GraphSAGE.

Achieving data fusion from various sources is challenging without violating users' confidentiality, largely due to the competing goals of data utilization and privacy protection. Differentially private techniques can be used to determine data access costs, which are necessary to assess data fusion costs. This paper utilizes a Huber approach to provide private insights into the structure of low-rank matrices, with the goal of estimating matrix norms to determine data fusion costs. The proposed method, which is based on the Huber loss, is privacy-preserving and sensitive to data accuracy, differing from traditional approaches. The framework is capable of estimating matrix norms with reduced privacy losses and is not directly comparable to previous methods using the Frobenius norm. The study validates the approach using real-world data and compares it to existing techniques.

We introduce a unified framework that integrates the effects of small dust particles, referred to as dust+PAH, to describe how dust influences the observation of interstellar continuum radiation, including the scattering and absorption of light, polarization, and specific emission features related to dust. This framework synthesizes the findings from numerous studies on interstellar dust, leveraging its uniformity to enable the interpretation of diverse observational data obtained across multiple wavelengths, polarization scales, and observational approaches. This framework provides a comprehensive understanding of interstellar radiation, including the scattering and absorption of light, polarization, and specific emission features related to dust. It synthesizes the findings from numerous studies on interstellar dust, leveraging its uniformity to enable the interpretation of diverse observational data obtained across multiple wavelengths, polarization scales, and observational approaches. This framework provides a solid foundation for the analysis of dust-related observations in various contexts, such as the study of interstellar radiation, the analysis of polarized starlight, the exploration of exoplanet atmospheres, and the comprehension of dust influence on the observation of celestial sources or the early universe.

The recently discovered, massive planet orbiting the low-mass star CIDA-1 has prompted a study of the planet's influence on its surrounding disk of dust. Analyzing data from the Spitzer Space Telescope, the researchers have identified a pattern of a ring-like structure with an inner limit beyond which the light cannot pass, characteristic of a gap created by a massive planet. They have also found that the planet has caused the formation of a power-law-like exoplanet tail with a specific slope. Considering CIDA-1's mass and age, the researchers have found that the planet's mass is substantial and its orbit has remained relatively unchanged since its formation. As a result, the researchers have concluded that CIDA-1's planet is an example of a massive planet capable of shaping and influencing the formation of planets and the surrounding material in protoplanetary disks. Moreover, the researchers have found that CIDA-1's planet has the potential to be seen using ground-based telescopes, making it a candidate for future studies of planetary migration and the reprocessing of material in disks surrounding extremely low-mass stars.

We investigate the most clicks needed to solve the Lights Out problem on infinite paths with a restriction of at most $k$ clicks. Our approach involves developing two click algorithms: one for general $k$, solving a specific integer equation, and another for odd $k$, leveraging a known decomposition. Our method also extends to finding the first unsatisfactory state in an $m$-stage instance, again limited by the $k$ click constraint. Lastly, we explore the relationship between the Lights Out problem and the Reachability problem in infinite timed automata, drawing a comparison to the undecidability of the problem when restricted to clicks.

This paper presents a novel approach to dividing an image into segments ($K$ parts) by combining it with a process for improving image clarity. The proposed model uses a specific mathematical formula that incorporates a detailed image representation ($\hat{y}$) and a partition of the image ($\{D_i\}$) to minimize costs associated with the division ($\div$) and the refinement ($\partial$) of the image. The model's key properties are proven, including its mathematical structure and behavior, and an efficient algorithm is developed to analyze these two interconnected processes. The effectiveness of the model is demonstrated through a series of numerical experiments focused on a variety of images.

To enhance the efficiency of Abstract Interpretation, this paper introduces a novel approach that separates the computation into distinct phases for over- and under-approximation, allowing for the reuse of approximate abstract domains during the analysis. The proposed technique combines the utilization of approximate and exact abstract domains to produce a more precise result. The development is facilitated by employing a basic Abstract Interpreter with an abstract domain capable of both over- and under-approximation. The presented case study showcases the potential benefits of this phase-decoupling approach in ABT-based Abstract Interpretation.

We investigate theoretically the optical properties of oxide perovskite crystals with tetragonal symmetry, focusing on the interaction between a dopant-induced vibrational mode and a nearby electronic transition. This analysis is highly relevant due to its proximity to an instability point where the vibrational mode transforms into a structural distortion and the system undergoes a significant phase transition. Two scenarios are considered, one involving a local vibrational mode coupling with a specific electronic state, resulting in an absorption spectrum characterized by a broad and blue-shifted peak, reminiscent of the observed absorption spectrum of titanates. We term this phenomenon geometric phonons governed by light. The other scenario involves a local vibrational mode and two electronic states, resulting in a broad and blue-shifted peak that weakens with time due to a decay of the local vibrational mode, a phenomenon we term light-controlled geometric phonons. The titanates offer a precise example, illustrating that geometric phonons governed by light can occur naturally.

Detecting anomalies in complex data is crucial across a rapidly expanding spectrum of applications. From visual surveillance to medical diagnosis and financial analysis, anomaly detection holds significant importance due to its potential to enhance overall performance. From both a practical and theoretical standpoint, it's well established that proximity-based methods can effectively identify anomalies based on the concept of closeness. However, these methods are often time-consuming and fail to provide precise results in certain cases. In this study, a novel approach to anomaly detection is proposed, utilizing a closeness graph called the Closeness Graph (CG) to efficiently and accurately identify anomalies in metric spaces. The CCG method employs two key components - the $k$-closest neighbor $(X, k)$ set and the distance $(X,r)$ set - to determine the closeness of data points and calculate their distance from the average distance, thereby identifying anomalies based on a predefined threshold. Our approach is validated through comprehensive empirical studies on real-world datasets, resulting in accurate and rapid anomaly detection across various metric spaces. Furthermore, a comparative analysis is conducted between the CG method and existing anomaly detection techniques, yielding promising outcomes.

The interaction between an atom and its surroundings can be observed through either radiation emitted due to electron spin flipping or through the atom's physical movement. An atom facing a mirror and undergoing oscillatory movement can cause stimulation of other atoms located nearby due to the atom's electromagnetic field, which can lead to radiation emission. An investigation is being conducted on an atom positioned perpendicular to a long, thin mirror to study how atom-mirror interaction affects the atom's emission of electromagnetic radiation. In this study, we consider the atom to be an oscillator vibrating at a specific frequency and calculate the radiation emitted due to the slab-mirror system. We find that the emitted radiation shows up as sharp, high-energy peaks within a specific range. These peaks correspond to the atom-slab system's resonant frequencies and can be observed on a specific branch of a Rabi spectrum. A comparison of these peaks' positions reveals that they correspond to specific processes: radiation emitted during the atom's movement (transient Rabi oscillations) and radiation emitted due to the atom and mirror reflecting light off each other (resonant amplification of radiation emitted during the atom's movement).

In the realm of social network analysis, our research focuses on measuring and evaluating equity within communities in large graphs. We introduce two statistical metrics: Local Equity Ratio and Local Equity Index, which both signify equity levels within neighborhoods of a graph. By combining these metrics with the presence of bridges, we identify and segment communities in the network. Our methods are extensively evaluated through 32 synthetic community structures and 5 real-world social networks, where we observe notable correlations between our analysis and the actual community segments, with a few notable discrepancies occurring in the analysis of real networks.

This research investigates the accuracy of numerical methods for a class of nonlinear equations that describe complex reversible enzyme reactions. Specifically, we analyze the behavior of iterative techniques such as the Newton-Raphson method and modified versions of it. By classifying these iterative methods as nonlinear solvers, we are able to apply Inclusion Principle-based techniques to develop modified Newton methods. These modified methods employ so-called "correction functions" to ensure the numerical solution remains within the feasible region. In the paper, we derive and analyze these correction functions for the specific case of a two-variable kinetic equation and show that they can be generalized to a broader class of nonlinear equations. Moreover, we establish the sufficient conditions for the convergence of iterative methods in the presence of correction functions, and provide numerical examples to demonstrate the effectiveness of these methods.

The research presents an investigation into supersymmetry, focusing on the $\sqrt{s} =$ 13 TeV LHC proton-proton collisions recorded by the CMS experiment, and reports results for the first time for certain supersymmetry scenarios where the squark masses differ significantly in the final states characterized by multiple jets, missing transverse momentum, and $b$-tagged jets. The study's findings are based on a dataset of 35.9 fb$^{-1}$ and consider various supersymmetry scenarios involving the lightest neutralino as a well-stable particle, and the squarks in the mass range of 300 to 600 GeV. The research further analyzes a distinct supersymmetry scenario known as chiral supersymmetry, where the squarks have significantly different masses, and the squark mass up to 1500 GeV. The study's findings are presented in the plane of beyond the standard model cross section and the efficiency to identify the plane of the missing transverse momentum.

In the field of mathematical finance, models have been created to simulate complex financial systems, including the probable outcomes of investment decisions. A new approach has been introduced to analyze investment risks, comprising three key components: the initial model, used to calculate the return on investment; a stochastic component, to assess potential risks; and a strategy to manage those risks. This framework has been tested and validated with real data from the financial market, specifically the stock prices of Apple Inc.

This work proposes a novel method to solve the quantum Harmonic Maser oscillator (QHMSO) equation, which involves deriving a specific expression utilizing a path integral technique and then employing Markov Chain Monte Carlo methods to obtain numerical solutions for key properties. To facilitate the computation, which is plagued by a high rejection rate due to non-physical proposal distributions, we developed an optimized algorithm. The method can be adapted to tackle more complex problems, such as a propelled quantum harmonic oscillator, which represents an advancement in applying Monte Carlo methods to condensed matter physics and related fields.

User reviews and ratings are crucial data for both item recommendation and review analysis, presenting either as separate entities or combined into a single document. While positive reviews often enhance product sales, negative reviews can deter potential buyers. Consequently, both positive and negative reviews are valuable for both item recommendation and review analysis.

Existing research on using reviews in recommendations has focused on either positive or negative reviews, but not both simultaneously. Combining review data necessitates handling the dual challenges of handling the quantity and quality of reviews, as well as their complementarity. This paper proposes the Sentiment-sensitve Interactive Fusion Network (SIFN), an approach to utilizing reviews for recommendations that considers review quantity and quality as well as the relationship between reviews and items. The proposed method is evaluated through experiments on two real-world datasets, showcasing its capability to outperform current state-of-the-art methods.

Data augmentation methods are used to boost the accuracy of NLP models by creating multiple copies of limited training data. Previous research has shown that automatic text manipulation can effectively increase model performance. This work presents ASMA, a novel data augmentation method that enhances Arabic-Eglish code-switched data with contextualized substitutions. We apply this technique to concrete part-switch operations, allowing words from one language to take the place of equivalent words in the other language. We compare the efficacy of different substitution techniques and find that simple string matching leads to better results. Our experiments demonstrate that ASMA boosts the accuracy of translation models, and our method outperforms existing data augmentation approaches.

We demonstrate that any infinite collection of surface homeomorphisms that are not topologically equivalent to the identity on compact subsets of the surface leads to a failure of precompactness according to the Hausdorff topology when the collection is restricted to all such subsets. Furthermore, this precompactness is specifically attributed to the group's action within the surface's homeotopy group, thereby establishing that any infinite subgroup exhibiting precompactness according to the Hausdorff topology must be conjugate to the subgroup generated by 1-dimensional Dehn twists. Additionally, this finding has the consequence that any infinite subgroup exhibiting precompactness according to the Roelcke topology cannot exist if it acts minimally, except in cases where it's within a surface that's identifiably equivalent to the circle.
