It's demonstrated that for all finite group G, having a virtually cyclic subgroup H, which is either isomorphic to a symmetric group S3 or an alternating group A4, all orbit equivalences that are consistent and stable, are also invariant to the unique action of G on an arbitrary set, making the category of G actions immovable and unchangeable under the operation of taking a transverse lift to a suitable group action framework. This finding particularly applies to the category of isometric actions on infinite dimensional Hilbert spaces by the solvable group SL2Z. Additionally, for the solvable group SL2Z acting on a 2 dimensional complex vector space, it's shown that all orbit equivalences are constant, and this work also establishes a full list of equivalent definitions for the category of isometric actions on a 2 dimensional real vector space by the solvable group SL2Z, showing that it's a particular type of immovable group action called inflexible.

This study examines various nonparametric methods for estimating a specific type of regression function, which takes into account both dependent and independent variables. Two methods, which involve data manipulation and kernel-based techniques, respectively, show that under certain conditions, these estimators converge at the same rate. Furthermore, nonparametric regression is also applied to time series data, and we investigate the rates of convergence for estimators based on moving average processes. Our analysis reveals that these estimators converge at the same rate. It's noted that a particular method of data manipulation can lead to biased estimates, which may be adjusted for through a complex adjustment procedure. Our findings suggest this adjustment actually produces an inconsistent estimator in some cases.

This research focuses on developing an observer for epidemiological models, which is a mathematical representation of the spread of infectious diseases. We introduce and apply the continuous extension principle to the control variable and unknown state variable, and subsequently derived and implemented to an epidemiological model commonly known as the SIRS model, which allows an infectious disease to convert and revert individuals. By constructing an observer for the SIRS model, we achieve accurate convergence of the estimated state to the actual state under certain conditions, which enables effective assessment and prediction of the disease state dynamics.

Recent advancements in temporal knowledge graph embedding have primarily centered on developing new models that combine static and temporal features. In this research, we explore an alternative strategy, in which we utilize a pre-trained static KGE model without modifying it, to predict edges within temporal knowledge graphs. To do this, we propose three methods for incorporating temporal information into a fixed model framework, based on different approaches to handling temporal features. The first method aligningly aggregates temporal vectors to represent the observed state, the second explicitly focuses on past and future vectors, and the third utilizes a temporal attention mechanism to weight past feature vectors more heavily when they are closer to the reference time. Experimental results demonstrate that our approach is competitive with state-of-the-art static KGE models and the recently proposed TKEE model for temporal knowledge graph embedding.

The process of Kerr-lens mode-locking in high-power Ti:Sa oscillators is crucial for producing extremely short and high-energy pulses. This paper provides a detailed analysis of the underlying physics driving Kerr-lens mode-locking in high-power oscillators. It delves into the role of spatial beam distortion and loss within the cavity, as well as the impact of nonlinear phase shift caused by the laser beam passing through the dye used in the Kerr lens. To validate the model, the researchers tested it against experimental data from an 88 MHz Ti:Sa oscillator producing 12 femtosecond pulses at 800nm. The results confirmed that the combination of fast electrical drivers and carefully calibrated balance in the laser design is necessary to achieve high performance.

A novel technique for nonlinear regression known as online federated learning (OLFE) has been proposed, which allows parallel training on various devices using a nonlinear model without a shared parameter space. However, a major challenge in OLFE remains managing resource disparities across devices. To tackle this, we have developed a resource-aware asynchronous OLFE framework (RAOAF). It works by enabling each device to adaptively control training duration based on local resources, thereby minimizing data imbalance. A novel asynchronous communication approach in RAOAF ensures a predictable OLFE convergence rate, which outperforms existing frameworks. Moreover, RAOAF converges at a similar rate to synchronous methods, despite asynchronous updates and resource disparities. To achieve this, RAOAF introduces a new objective function and analytical guarantees it for nonlinear regression. A real-world experiment using real-world data demonstrates RAOAF's superiority over competing methods, which is further shown through simulations using real resource data.

To enhance the absorption of thin silicon layers, 3D photonic band gap back reflectors were created using colloidal sphere crystal structures. By adjusting the sphere size, various photonic band gaps with different wavelengths can be produced. Experiments involving silicon wafers with reduced thickness (between 100nm and 300nm) were conducted to observe absorption improvements. Using spectroscopic ellipsometry, absorption spectra of thin silicon layers were compared to theoretical simulations from MRS-Tiny. The results revealed that thin silicon layers with 12-period colloidal crystal reflectors exhibited higher absorption at specific wavelengths compared to bare thin layers. An improvement in absorption of 33% was seen at 220nm thickness and 5.5 periods, exceeding the theoretical limit. However, the proposed method failed to yield improved absorption in thicker silicon layers (above 200nm).

We design a computational algebra system that solves the fundamental algebra equation $x^{(u+1)}=x^u \cdot x$. This solution is then used to optimize various tetration formulas, specifically to compute $a^{((n-1)\cdot m)}$ for a given $a$. Our method aspires to expand our knowledge of how the number system works, yet it exhibits a significant shortcoming by only producing approximate solutions rather than exact ones.

Measures of functional efficiency for covered areas provide a basis for determining the optimal number of infill points needed for accurate geographical surveys. We've established a new method for precisely estimating the required fill-in amount, which also allows us to construct enhanced geometric coverings. This method involves using a geometric covering of a given metric space and its associated functional process to calculate an efficiency measure. Notably, this approach can be applied even when the functional process doesn't satisfy certain conditions necessary for classical statistical inference. Furthermore, our method is practical and has real-world applications, as its complementarity to classical sampling procedures allows for accurate infill decisions. We've also adapted this technique for use in higher dimensional settings, proposing new coverings for Rd+1 for any d ≥ 1, which can be used with a given finite functional process. Interestingly, our method for geometric constructions depends on the specific metric chosen for the input space. As such, we've established a new class of functions, which we call 'Lipschitz cocovers,' which are associated with a specific metric and provide a universally applicable method for determining the required fill-in amount.

GdInO$_3$ possesses an unique honeycomb crystal structure featuring a high spin polarization fraction of nearly 3.5 times that of any other known material. This study focuses on the magnetic properties of a nearly two-dimensional honeycomb lattice in GdInO$_3$. Long-range magnetic order is investigated through comprehensive structural analysis on single-crystal samples, combined with magnetization and heat capacity measurements. A detailed theoretical analysis incorporating quantum effects is performed using a mean-field model based on the J$_1$-J$_{\infty}$ Heisenberg Hamiltonian. These findings demonstrate that GdInO$_3$ is the first material to exhibit a magnetic ground state within the same type of compounds.

Predicting connections in large networks is an important issue, particularly in life sciences where understanding relationships can lead to crucial insights. The main challenge lies in striking a balance between making accurate predictions and managing the resources required to process vast datasets. To address this issue, a novel approach called SSNE (Similarity-based Shortest Path Negative Embedded network with friends) is proposed, addressing link prediction in sparse networks. SSNE transforms the link prediction problem by creating negative examples based on the number of available network connections. It then applies node embedding using a unique approach that incorporates edge similarities into node representations. Specifically, it uses the shortest path to calculate the similarity of each connection, transforming this information into high-dimensional vector representation. SSNE uses a unique approach to convert negative examples into low-dimensional vector representation by selecting the top connections for each node, effectively reducing the resources required. It then applies a single neural network to predict the existence of relationships between nodes. To further improve efficiency, SSNE uses color clustering to reduce the size of the network. Experiments show that SSNE performs well in real-world scenarios, effectively predicting relationships in networks it has been trained on. The approach is highly efficient, effectively processing networks of any size.

We introduce a novel atomic vapor chamber technology that incorporates deep silicon features on microelectromechanical systems (MEMS) devices. This innovative approach utilizes a device chip as the containment chamber for the vaporized atoms. In this study, we outline the general principles and details of our atomic vapor chamber fabrication. We present measurements of the chambers' characteristics, including the alkali metal atom density, the dark resonance linewidth, and the Stark shift. We also demonstrate a method to optimize the vapor chamber's atom density by adjusting the chamber's temperature. This technology offers the potential for the integration of atomic physics experiments with cutting-edge integrated microsystems, enhancing interaction and coupling between atoms and electronic circuits.

We analyze the effectiveness of a model that calculates nonlinear disruption power, which occurs when interacting dual-polarization 4D signals encounter random nonlinear channels. The model's findings align closely with simulations of specific examples, including a serum link example, at a 10 Gbit/s transmission level.

Recent years have seen an alarming rise in wildfires caused by a combination of climate change, weather conditions, and human activities, resulting in devastating effects on the environment. Wildfire prevention efforts are typically hindered by the use of low-light level infrared cameras due to visibility constraints. An innovative solution can be devised by leveraging the strengths of both infrared and visible spectrum images, taken by cameras with different wavelengths, to generate high-quality color images for effective wildfire monitoring. 

The proposed FIRe-GAN, a novel deep learning-based approach, has been successfully applied to the combined use of low-light level infrared and visible spectrum images, enabling the generation of high-quality color images for wildfire visualization. Composed of two primary components, the IR-VI decoder produces a combined image with the infrared properties of one image and the color tone of the other, while the color enhancement module refines the output to create more visually appealing images. 

The performance of FIRe-GAN was evaluated using a diverse dataset consisting of 150,000 image pairs from multiple locations, showcasing its adaptability. The application of FIRe-GAN to real-world images has been demonstrated, along with a comprehensive performance comparison to other state-of-the-art image fusion techniques. The results indicate the substantial potential of FIRe-GAN to revolutionize the field of image-based wildfire monitoring and prevention. 

The study also identified a range of potential avenues for further research, including the extension of FIRe-GAN to support multiple images, the adaptation of the model

While numerous tools to analyze mental health from social media content have been explored, the underlying data and training methodologies used often remain undisclosed, hindering replication and validation. To address this, a well-structured approach for collecting and evaluating dataset patterns, which may indicate depression, is presented. A dataset comprising 1,000 Facebook post instances was developed, along with several training and testing methodologies, including neural network and natural language processing analyses, to identify reliable indicators of depression. The dataset and results, which include an average of 3.0 predicted labels and analysis of comment quantity on Facebook posts, have shown promising indicators, such as number of comments and post text analysis. The dataset and findings are available for public access, aiming to facilitate replication and improvement of depression detection methods.

To analyze the COVID-19 pandemic, a dynamic, probabilistic model is developed that accounts for the virus's transmission, testing, and varying individual behaviors in response to information about the disease and government restrictions. Simulation outcomes based on Chicago area data demonstrate that this model accurately recreates the real-world dynamics observed during the pandemic's initial stages. Additionally, the model's predictive capabilities, combined with parameter adjustability, allow for hypothetical scenarios to be simulated and assessed. For instance, the model's forecasts are significantly improved when social distancing measures are implemented compared to when they are not. Furthermore, the model shows that inconsistent testing and behaviors among individuals with the same average knowledge can lead to a wide disparity in outbreak severity levels.

To examine the coupling between the isoscalar monopole (IS0) and quadrupole (IS2) resonances, the isoscalar sum rules related to the E0 and E2 transitions are calculated for $^{24}$Mg and $^{28}$Si using the configurations obtained from the extreme skewness limit theory. The strength of the E0 and IS2 sum rule is found, and the reduced E0 transition matrix element and E2 sum rule strength are determined. The reduced E0 transition matrix element for $^{24}$Mg and $^{28}$Si is calculated, and the E2 sum rule strength for $^{24}$Mg and $^{28}$Si along with the E0$ \rightarrow $E2 coupling in $^{24}$Mg and $^{28}$Si is assessed. The gyromagnetic ratios for magnetic dipole and electric dipole transitions are calculated, and the large IS0 strength at the experimental energy in $^{24}$Mg along with the E0 $\rightarrow $E2 coupling in $^{24}$Mg and $^{28}$Si is revealed.

The stick-slip phenomenon, often observed in systems manipulated by a force with a low friction coefficient, is similar to that seen in biological motor control systems. These systems feature a motor producing a force that opposes a load, and controlled by a feedback mechanism that adjusts the motor's position. The motor's behavior is influenced by two factors: a force that mimics a muscle contraction, and friction that opposes the motor's movement. Research into these systems has revealed they can facilitate fast and accurate movements, even with low friction levels, unlike initial predictions. Instead of sliding being preferred over sticking, it has been discovered that they are interchangeable states, dependent on the system's history and the forces at play. A key discovery was that the absence of a friction threshold can lead to the occurrence of attractors that cause the system to get stuck in perpetual motion, a state that can be overcome with the application of sufficient muscle force to break the cycle.

Time series forecasting, like assessing stock prices or the spread of a virus, involves predicting future values for a given variable based on past data. However, because these predictions are always uncertain, the uncertainty also has a significant impact. Bellman equation-based time series forecasting methods, which include many well-known techniques such as dynamic time series models and neural networks, often struggle to account for uncertainty. We introduce a new approach called profound Bellman management (PBM), specifically designed to minimize the risk associated with uncertainty in time series forecasting. By using a manage-and-learn framework that incorporates both the forecasting model and a separate management model, PBM mitigates uncertainty. During training, PBM reduces the risk associated with uncertainty by adjusting the management model; surprisingly, this approach also improves the performance of the forecasting model. We show that PBM can effectively manage uncertainty and significantly improve the results for a wide range of tasks, including many types of time series forecasting.

In today's interactive environment, recommender systems utilize suggested items to grab users' attention. To deliver the most relevant recommendations possible, they rely on a precise understanding of the user's intent. However, deciphering users' underlying intent proves to be an intricate task, especially when considering their dynamic intent which can shift over time. To address this challenge, this study proposes a novel framework called the Hidden User Intent Framework. This approach consists of two key models - a User Intent HMM where user intent transitions are hidden and a Recommendation Framework - to address the challenge of allocating items to users based on their likely intent. The framework showcases its effectiveness through its performance in a publicly available game platform, where it significantly outperforms existing sequential recommenders, resulting in a 27% boost in click-through rates and 41% boost in flow-through rates.

The paper starts with an analysis of the solution space of the SDCHE, considering the general form of the equation $x^2y''+xy'+y=\frac{\lambda^3(\lambda+1)}{q(4p+q)}x^4+\frac{\lambda^2}{q}x^2+f(\frac{\lambda}{x})$. The paper shows that the solution space of the SDCHE corresponds to the subset of the SFO that consists of functions with a zero of infinite order. This study establishes lower bounds for the eigenvalue gap in a rank-one matrix evaluation, where each group's matrix can vary freely and the others are set to zero. Relevant applications include the analysis of homogeneous submatrices and the eigenvalue counting in the partitioned Laplacian of a graph.

Several network topological properties are too heavily influenced by the central positions of key nodes, which makes them unreliable for networks lacking symmetry. To overcome this issue, a new network topological property has been developed, using edge connections instead of node connections. This property provides a more stable insight into networks lacking symmetry. As examples, the essential topological properties of two biological networks, CBS and Taulife, have been calculated, demonstrating its capability to detect stable network patterns in these networks.

We present a novel observable, denoted as $R_{LFU}$, quantifying Semi-inclusive Lepton Flavor Equivalence (LFE) in $b\to s\ell^+\ell^-$ transitions. This observable, formulated as the ratio of Equivalence to Polarization components to the $K^*$ transverse momentum, enables a comprehensive characterization of LFE within the $K^*$ meson decay mode. As $R_{LFU}$ is insensitive to most tensor and vector form factors influenced by QCD, it is primarily governed by electroweak form factors. Given that certain $CP$-violating and flavour-changing neutral current effects do not affect $R_{LFU}$, it becomes a valuable tool for extracting $|G_{S/T}_{LEP}(0)|^2$ and cross-checking against polarisation modes, ultimately aiding in understanding $b\to s$ transitions at zero momentum transfer and with minimal QCD effects interference. This insight can further be applied to other processes, such as $B\to K\ell^+\ell^-$, with a similar approach.

This research explores decentralized active network management in linear systems with interconnected multi-channel architecture. We reframe the problem of network coordination to minimize a cost function as an optimization issue, providing a numerical solution that achieves optimal outcomes. To apply this optimization solution in practice, we examine the stability of the resulting decentralized control system and show that it consists of independently controlled separate channels. We derive a set of necessary conditions for stability and provide a practical distributed algorithm based on those requirements, ensuring consistent behavior of the algorithm across different starting points. The approach is "plug-and-play," enabling seamless integration of new nodes without recalibration, and preserving convergence even in the presence of delays. We demonstrate our approach with a realistic example of power networks.

To combat the rapid spread of COVID-19, accurate diagnosis and treatment depend on various molecular and imaging tests. Bypassing the need for physical samples and reducing the risk of infection for healthcare professionals, molecular and imaging tests have become essential. This research proposes a two-phase approach, comprised of predictive analytics and rule-based analysis, to categorize COVID-19 patients based on omics data. Utilizing the 86 categories of omics data defined by the WHO, our method ensures that all patients are assigned a category and undergoes strict privacy protocols. This approach leverages the BERT-NLP model to extract meaningful insights from unstructured medical text reports, thereby facilitating the categorization of patients. In addition, we demonstrate the effectiveness of our rules-based system in assigning categories to patients, while ensuring that all patients are accurately categorized. This research presents findings on the application of machine learning to medical text analysis, highlighting its potential to aid in the diagnosis and treatment of patients.

Network effects have become a crucial aspect of modern research, impacting both academic and industrial advancements. In this context, in-depth understanding and mathematical analysis of network properties that produce these effects are highly valuable. This comprehensive guide serves as a foundational network theory framework, providing young researchers with a strong base to approach their work in the field of network analysis. It covers fundamental concepts, discussion of influential models and theories, and mathematical modeling to address various network-related problems, focusing particularly on topics where no clear consensus exists. It delves into topics such as epidemic networks, attack and defense strategies, search methods, and online diffusion, using a first-class operator approach. This approach not only offers a straightforward linear method for analysis but also enables exploring non-linear problems by employing approximate solutions. With a clear distinction between the guide's focus on theoretical networks and real-world applications, it explores topics such as link prediction, community structure, network visualization, and related problems. With a strong emphasis on providing young researchers with a toolkit to develop, improve, and apply network theory, this guide positions its authors as leading experts in the field, offering them a platform to showcase their expertise and share their knowledge to drive future advancements.

In 2009, Gudelj and colleagues introduced the concept of eco-evolutionary dynamics, occurring within specific timeframes, as a convergence of evolutionary changes and feedback mechanisms affecting ecology. Since then, research has largely focused on the implications of eco-evolutionary dynamics, rather than defining its temporal boundaries. Our study investigates the transition from traditional evolutionary dynamics to modern eco-evolutionary dynamics by mathematically defining the eco-evolutionary dynamics process and examining its progression from initial to extended timeframes. Within these timeframes, we identify various regimes of eco-evolutionary dynamics, influenced by parameters such as initial conditions, parameters, and system characteristics. Our analysis demonstrates that eco-evolutionary dynamics can exhibit complex patterns, including bistability and chaos, particularly in multi-parameter systems. In contrast, lower-dimensional evolutionary systems tend to display more ordered behavior, such as stable states and limit cycles. In general, eco-evolutionary dynamics tends to show increased complexity as it operates within longer timeframes, often exhibiting increased sensitivity to initial conditions. Our research suggests that eco-evolutionary dynamics, particularly in its extended timeframe, may be better represented by chaotic theory, exemplified by the generalized Hénon map.

Successful self-supervised learning of speech patterns is crucial for developing accurate speech recognition technologies. To better understand how speech training affects our ability to interpret speech, we conducted a study with human listeners who were either trained self-supervisedly using unobstructed speech or artificially degraded speech. Our results show that artificially obstructing the speech patterns makes them more challenging for humans to recognize, and this counterintuitive phenomenon increases as the degree of obstruction rises. To further analyze this contradictory relationship between speech education and recognition difficulty, we examined the listening capabilities of both educated individuals with normal hearing and those with hearing impairments. Notably, individuals with hearing impairments showed a comparable pattern of difficulty in recognizing speech patterns, even at different frequencies of obstruction. Our research also suggests that this contradictory relationship can be explained by an inverse variation principle, and by modeling the trade-offs between speech education and recognition difficulty, we can refine this inverse variation principle.

This study offers a thorough examination of the characteristics that drive the adoption and performance of blockchain-powered decentralized exchanges. Adoption potential is evaluated through the lens of the Ansoff Matrix, a framework for assessing levels of risk and change. Performance, on the other hand, is analyzed based on the economic principles of economic survival, growth, and prosperity. Based on the insights from experts and literature review, a comprehensive model is proposed that incorporates nine key factors, consisting of risk, complexity, network effects, competition, reputation, security, governance, portability, and transparency. Subsequently, a binary classification model is developed to forecast whether a decentralized exchange will achieve economic survival by predicting its binary success within a specified timeframe. The predicted outcomes are evaluated through multiple metrics, including accuracy, F1 score, and ROC values. Notably, the proposed model achieves satisfactory classification performance with a high F1 score of 0.175, suggesting promising results. Furthermore, a survival analysis is conducted using the Kaplan-Meier estimator from the perspective of the token holders, revealing a concerning pattern of frequent project abandonment by the token holders, with approximately 80% of projects achieving economic failure within two years.

To address the common issue of missing data in studies on medical devices, we introduce a new sensitivity analysis within the Bayesian framework. The approach builds on existing methods, such as the E-value, to determine if findings hold when key assumptions are violated due to unobserved data. While traditional sensitivity analyses focus on altering study outcomes, we utilize a Bayesian technique to assess unobserved data, thus identifying potential issues before conducting the analysis. To facilitate this analysis, we provide guidance on performing a Bayesian sensitivity analysis and offer a computational tool for practical application.

The potential benefits of Internet of Vehicles (IoV) on autonomous driving have garnered significant interest from researchers, who anticipate that Internet of Vehicles technology will revolutionize the way vehicles interact with each other and their surroundings. To address concerns about data security and privacy, researchers suggest the use of secure data exchange mechanisms. To address these needs, a blockchain-enabled framework for federated learning has been proposed, allowing vehicles to share data within their local environments while maintaining centralized control over privacy. To realize this vision, a blockchain-enabled framework for federated learning has been proposed, allowing vehicles to share data within their local environments while maintaining control over privacy. To advance this goal, a blockchain-enabled framework for federated learning has been proposed, allowing vehicles to share data within their local environments. To develop this vision, a comprehensive survey of literature has been conducted, a modular structure that has been adopted.

Charmonia production in proton-proton collisions at intermediate energy levels has been studied by the ALICE detector for central events with a total energy of 5.02 TeV. This research analyzed data on D0, D+, and D*+ mesons in relation to parton scattering at different impact parameters, and found that charm particles created near the event's center produce more fragments than those produced in peripheral collisions. A simulation of these findings with a specific model of particle interaction confirmed that charm particles formed at the event's center release more fragments than those produced in peripheral collisions. This research found that particles such as D0, D+, and D*+ have similar rates of being produced in central and non-central collisions, and that they primarily exist as direct mesons, with very little existing as non-prompt hadrons. A separate analysis of beauty hadroproduction discovered that beauty hadrons have a higher rate of fragmentation in central collisions and that they primarily exist as direct beauty hadrons, with very little existing as non-direct beauty hadrons. This research found that beauty hadrons have a higher rate of fragmentation in central collisions. A separate analysis of the production of all observed hadrons, including those from beauty and charm quarks, showed that they primarily exist as direct mesons, with very little existing as non-direct hadrons. To develop reliable quantum computers, it is vital to test them at extremely low temperatures in a specially controlled environment. Quantum-bit (qubit) error rates must fall below 10 to 20 errors per minute to enable large-scale computations. We have developed an advanced cryogenic system capable of maintaining temperatures well below 500 millikelvin in a matter-of-minutes timeframe, achieving a stability of 50 millikelvin without additional insulation. The system can support multiple users and features remote access, allowing for seamless cooperation in quantum-computer testing. It can also be evacuated to 30 nanopascals, eliminating heat transfer from helium ions, and qubit performance can be monitored remotely using quantum-bit techniques.

Real-time feedback from the public is essential for understanding how various social media-related tasks, such as routing, affect local communities, as evidenced by the destruction caused by false information during the Ebola outbreak in Sierra Leone. A key requirement for precise urban modeling is a complete dataset of street names. Typically, this information is accessible through publicly available sources like OpenStreetMap, yet it can become inaccurate if there's a discrepancy between the data and the actual scene, which necessitates manual correction. A feasible solution is automated polling station feedback, which has been hindered by the labor-intensive process of collecting and individual annotation of such feedback. In this research, we present WORTH, a real-world experimentation platform targeting urban feedback, which utilizes a large bank of IP cameras linked to digital signage to automatically capture and analyze feedback, as well as employ reinforcement learning to prioritize and manage the collection of street name feedback. A set of 8000 miles of routing feedback data collected over a period of three years show the potential benefits, as well as the challenges, of crowd-sourcing feedback, which include the impact of noise and variability. WORTH's primary goal is to automatically transcribe the feedback using deep learning for street name extraction, which has been successful in 57% of the test cases, according to human validation. Following this, the extracted feedback is used to update the graph model of the city, which has led to the update of 65% of the street name tags in the graph.

In various fields, including geophysical and medical imaging, the objective of sparse model deconvolution is to reconstruct a limited-view target function with a few significant components. This paper introduces a novel sparse model called the Nonuniform Sparse Analysis Network (NuSPAN), which comprises a proxi-mean network, enabling a highly adaptable and efficient analysis dictionary via a single learnable matrix. The NuSPAN model's optimization can be efficiently resolved through an iterative algorithm with a computationally efficient convergence guarantee. The proposed method's effectiveness is demonstrated through numerical simulations based on seismic data, seismic synthetic data, and real-world applications in seismic inversion.

This research explores the semigroups composed of composition operators associated with various analytic functions possessing certain norm control behaviors on the unit circle. By employing generalized Muckenhoupt type conditions, a class of norms denoted by $\mathcal{M}_{\sigma}$ is introduced, enabling the semigroups in question to meet specific integral operator conditions within spaces akin to BMOA. As the condition $\mathcal{M}_\sigma$ encompasses the Muckenhoupt p-condition, several notable categories of analytic functions possessing this condition are retrieved as special cases, inclusive of those functions characterized by a single real number. Moreover, under a specified assumption, a particular subcategory of beta-transformation functions characterized by integer values is shown to satisfy the semigroup integral operator condition in question.

We formulate an operator amalgamation method relevant to wavefunction overlaps with a specified symmetry, derive short-term limitations and a universal correction for the overlap's squared magnitude, and demonstrate its utility in calculating the overlap for the Haagerup model's ground state.

Automating the annotation of large quantities of past writings into parts-of-speech is crucial for enabling effective use of past literatures in tasks including language analysis, reconstruction, and understanding. Nevertheless, relying solely on current automatic annotation tools is not sufficient, especially in contexts where there is a lack of high-quality, human-provided annotations available. In this research, a novel framework is proposed for dependable parts-of-speech annotation. This framework utilizes a specific machine learning technique known as set-valued neural networks, which is capable of predicting multiple possible annotations for a given text, along with their associated levels of confidence. By leveraging the collection of annotated text samples that have been prepared by human experts, and incorporating the use of sampling-based methods to balance out class biases, the framework is capable of gradually improve the accuracy of its predictions over time. Experimental results indicate that the framework is capable of making reliable parts-of-speech annotations in contexts where the available annotated data is limited, as evidenced by its performance on past collections of writings.

The absence of smoothness in real-world data often hinders its usability for machine learning applications. However, an area of machine learning research, non-smooth integrability, offers a framework for determining how to combine information despite real-world data's lack of smoothness. This research, to our knowledge, formally defines non-smooth integrability for the first time, providing a rigorous mathematical framework. A novel loss function is proposed, along with a non-smooth generalization of the concept of invariance and robustness. The paper also introduces a new concept called semi-invariance and offers both smooth and non-smooth formulations for it. Experimental validation of the proposed methods and their performance on non-smooth data have been demonstrated.

As technology advances, especially in sectors like healthcare and education, 
disadvantaged communities are given the chance to catch up by utilizing modern
helpful systems. However, setting realistic expectations is crucial to avoid
disappointment. Disappointment in this case may lead to severe consequences and
strains on relationships between the city of Amsterdam and the companies it works
with. To prevent such outcomes and manage these relationships, an open dialogue
should take place, during which the city's expectations from these companies
should be clearly outlined. To achieve this, a tool has been developed that 
helps companies understand and manage the expectations set by the city in a 
more formal and structured manner. This tool was tested in a workshop with 
representatives from various tech companies, yielding positive results. The 
project's open-source code and documentation are accessible at a specific URL.

We suggest using the concealed inverses protocol to describe a specific noise model that incorporates inverse processes and shows that it effectively minimizes errors caused by noise in quantum information, particularly in systems that rely on superconducting quantum electronics. The hidden inverse process represents a form of system self-correction that can tackle challenges posed by noise in quantum information, an issue that has sparked significant debate in the field. The hidden inverse process enables the development of self-correcting codes that can circumvent second-order errors, an advantage of certain decoding techniques. We provide detailed mathematical explanations and illustrate the underlying physical mechanisms in the context of superconducting quantum electronics, an emerging technology in quantum computing.

The concept of preorder can be dynamically visualized through the cocartesian depiction in discrete categories. This visualization serves as a robust equivalent to the traditional order diagram. We uncover the essential requirements necessary for a category to effectively portray preorders, which essentially boils down to identifying the category's ability to be fully covered by the category's morphisms. In the context of regular categories, equivalence connections serve as a potential substitute for binary relations in constructing preorder diagrams. However, current literature falls short in providing a sufficient condition for the existence of such an equivalence relation within the framework of any regular category. We address this gap by establishing that the presence of atomic monos ensures the existence of an equivalence relation capable of representing preorder diagrams within a regular category.

To analyze the intricate connection between large marine events and their spatial patterns, we developed a multivariate spatial model for extreme values. This model takes into account the correlation between high marine events, as well as the spatial trends in these events. To manage complex relationships, we employed a non-linear transformation using a specialized function based on the "inverted Gaussian" distribution, which can better capture extreme value patterns. Additionally, we used a flexible, spatial-based approach to handle dependencies between different marine events. To handle the challenges associated with our approach, we used an advanced computational method with guaranteed results. Extensive analysis is performed using simulated data to assess the performance of our approach. To model extreme marine events, we apply our method to real-world data from the North Sea, which is used to estimate and visualize extreme water level values in the region.

To enhance visual-language models' understanding of text contexts, a new task called Visual-texts Text Explanation (VTE) has been developed. This task involves predicting an image-based explanation for a given text, requiring a model to deeply comprehend both the image content and the text's semantic meaning. The VT-CLIP model, introduced in this research, combines VIT and multi-cropped CLIP with additional context-aware comparison modules, to effectively tackle the VTE challenge. On the newly introduced large-scale VTE dataset, VT-CLIP has demonstrated superior performance compared to other prominent vision-language models. Moreover, this research shows that by incorporating the VTE task, a significant improvement can be achieved in other key applications, like visual-directed text editing. The proposed VTE task, VT-CLIP approach, and associated datasets are made publicly available to facilitate future research in this area.

To effectively compute the inverse of a perturbed matrix, we develop a universal strategy compatible with various types of noise. The key element is a specific family of functions with optimal robustness properties, which are implicitly leveraged through the integration of operator switching into the tensor product renormalization procedure. The efficacy of this approach is demonstrated by applying it to systems affected by random noise and comparing the results to numerical simulations.

We introduce the concept of segments of quaternionic spectra, characterized by special types of extensions between spectrally-enriched categories. Given a finite abelian group, G, we focus on the category of G-quaternionic spectra, which forms the foundational part of a larger system. The study of these spectral extensions serves as an advanced aspect of quaternionic homological algebra. The paper demonstrates that when G is a direct result of the group formations {2, 4}_{\infty}, this category becomes fully encompassing. The employed methodology involves utilizing the categories of matrix and T-spectra to illustrate spectral extensions.

Given a specific set of conditions involving $d$, $k$, and $\mathcal{F}$, we derive an expression for calculating the $h_d^{set}$ value of a $k$-algebra $R$ in terms of $\mathcal{F}$-pure thresholds and $F$-ring properties, provided that $R$ is a local $k$-algebra with $(R,\pi)$ and $h_{d-1}^{set} \leq \mathcal{F}(R) < \infty$. This result generalizes the existing $h_1^{set}$ case proved by Alper and Pyaghov in 2020.

The application of machine learning in image analysis is gaining momentum, with the medical imaging community working to establish standardized practices for image modification and machine learning workflows to facilitate widespread adoption. To support this effort, we introduce Highdicom, an open-source Python framework that provides a structured approach to defining image processing and machine learning workflows, enabling users to define image metadata, mapping procedures, and machine learning model results in DICOM format. By utilizing Highdicom, users can create a consistent dataset of images and corresponding annotations, which can then be converted to DICOM format for sharing and collaborative purposes. Highdicom is accompanied by two sample projects, which illustrate its functionality in image analysis for histopathology and radiology applications.

We start with a general idea that any factor $\lambda^s$ where $s\neq0$ can be expressed as the surface integral of $\frac{1}{2\lambda} \textbf{H}$ over some space volume, where $\textbf{H}$ represents the Hamiltonian density. This understanding is then used to derive the connection between Einstein-Hilbert action, surface Einstein-Hilbert action and Virasoro algebra through Noether charge calculation. This enables us to arrive at Virasoro algebra from the time-time component of the expectation value of Noether charge by setting $\lambda$ as the scale factor of the space. As a byproduct, we obtain an expression for entropy based on surface area, which can also be seen as the expectation value of Noether charge's energy component. This can be viewed as an extension of the earlier findings by Ghosh and Sunderaraman [1], [2], which were also discussed in Bhattacharya and Banerjee [3]. Our current analysis aligns with the later thoughts by Singh [4].

In the field of genomics, extensive DNA sequences have been found, yet the majority remain uninterpreted due to limited resources and difficulty in identifying significant data patterns within them. To aid in understanding complex DNA patterns, researchers employ machine learning techniques, particularly for large datasets where analysis is impractical without automated tools. To address this challenge, a novel, unsupervised machine learning framework has been developed, enabling effective representation of DNA sequences through an unsupervised learning method of neural networks. The proposed system, named DNA-Net, captures unique characteristics inherent in sequences, outperforming current methods as validated on real-world viral and bacterial genome datasets.

V$_2$O$_3$ is a correlated electron system that undergoes a metal-to-insulator transition dependent on crystal strain and oxidation conditions. Our study investigates how the surface conditions of V$_2$O_3$(0001)$ thin films, prepared on Re and W substrates, influence their metal/insulator state at room temperature at varying air pressures. When pressed against Re substrates with a smaller lattice constant, the transformation from insulating to metallic state occurs at atmospheric pressure, as typically seen for bulk V$_2$O_3$. In contrast, films deposited directly on W substrates with a larger lattice constant remain insulating even at high pressure and exhibit a distinct metal/insulating transition at pressure thresholds of 10$^{-7}$ and 10$^{-3}$ Torr. These findings suggest that the primary factor limiting metallic conductivity in V$_2$O_3$ films is the presence of a vapor layer on their surface, which can be avoided by using a surface treatment involving a high-temperature reduction in hydrogen. This treatment not only enhances electronic conductivity in V$_2$O_3$ films but also completely replaces the WO$_6$ surface layer typically formed on W substrates to a W(V, O) layer rich in vanadium.

We investigate the Lie-Poisson equation for algebra-friendly groups, demonstrating that solutions to this equation within the algebra's comultiplication-invariant subset are in concert with the group's Clebsch variables. This result facilitates a translation of the equation into an equivalent canonical Hamiltonian form on the group's dual space. The new formulation enables a straightforward conversion of known results between the two variable systems. Notably, we explore the properties of integrability, complete integrability, and monotonicity in both variable systems for Lie-Poisson equations.

This study presents detailed analysis and radial velocity measurements for 28
micro-lensing planets identified by KMTNet in 2018 in the sub-prime field, which
enables us to evaluate the anomalies of these planets in relation to their
host stars' characteristics. Out of the 28 planets, 25 show significant planetary
mass ratios and all but one planet have notable (differences greater than 3σ) 
anomalies, with eight planets exhibiting significant discrepancies in their
residual peak heights, indicating potential low-mass companions or multiple-lensing
anomalies. Moreover, 25 of the 28 planets have observed metallicity data for their
host stars and 21 have reliable estimates, with 19 of these exhibiting
significantly anomalous planetary mass ratios. By combining our findings with
literature data, we found no correlation between planetary anomalies and their host
stars' characteristics, and 17 out of 28 show anomalies, with 9 exhibiting
significantly anomalous peak shapes. Our study provides new insights into the
relationship between planetary mass ratios and their host stars' metallicity.

This study is a follow-up to a previous investigation focusing on significant outcomes derived using the minimum entropy principle for incompressible fluid flows. To expand the scope of applications for this principle, we demonstrate its substantial results for incompressible fluid flows to be a subset of those for their compressible counterparts. Moreover, novel entropy-dissipation rate estimates for compressible flows are obtained under specific symmetry conditions on the flow domain.

This paper identifies and assesses several supervised machine learning algorithms suitable for natural product linkage prediction, a task of predicting whether two chemicals are connected based on their structural data. Six classes of algorithms were examined, including decision tree-based, linear and nonlinear model sets, as well as neural network and KNN classes. Among the analyzed methods, a specific type of decision tree and two artificial neural network classes demonstrated the best performance in pairwise link prediction, achieving an overall accuracy of 85% and 80.83% respectively, on a dataset with 219,952 pairs. Furthermore, a self-developed method was employed to investigate the importance of specific chemical compound features, enabling the identification of crucial characteristics for link prediction tasks.

We define a variant of Dyck trails called colorful Dyck trails that incorporate color mappings, and use them to develop a corresponding family of colorful symmetric functions in terms of q-analogs of single-set generating functions for these trails. Additionally, we establish a connection between colorful Dyck trails and q-rook theory on extended Dyck paths, resulting in a push-button inventory analogous to the MacMahon's formula, and providing two approaches to derive the Dyck and Excluded Box formulas from it.

In computer vision, particularly when dealing with orientation-independent object recognition, convolutional networks often require substantial data augmentation to simulate various object rotations. This process can be costly and leads to a significant demand for computer power. To mitigate these issues, this research introduces a new set of convolutional networks called Orientation Convolutional Networks (OCN). These networks are specifically designed to bypass the need for data augmentation for object orientation independence. Additionally, OCN architectures are constructed using a novel type of convolutional layer called a Circular Average Pooling (CAP) layer. This CAP layer is unique in that it replicates the outcome of averaging pooling but with a key difference: it enables the preservation of that information. We test the effectiveness of our OCN architectures through numerous experiments involving a range of applications including multi-oriented digit recognition, digit classification within MNIST, Fashion MNIST, and SVHN datasets. Our findings indicate that the OCN models outperform the baseline Convolutional Network (CNN) model across all the mentioned applications.

We develop a novel framework to compute a type of average, referred to as relative trace, for functions on domains with complex geometries, encompassing reals, complexes, and quaternions. Building on this, we establish a new equation type, referred to as the relative trace equation, which facilitates a broader interpretation of the relative trace. In doing so, we introduce the concepts of curved linear intervals and a generalization of interval linear programming that can be applied to these constructs. This equation type can be used to optimize problems defined on such geometries and has applications in computing quantities for fields with non-zero characteristic exponents. Our approach relies on a generalized representation of the field, referred to as a split-field, and the use of curves in these domains, referred to as split-curve, which hold distinct properties depending on whether they enter or exit the unit circle.

The mass of the top quark plays a significant role in numerous theoretical models beyond the standard model that involve significant interactions with the top quark. To establish robust constraints on these models, effective parameters derived from top quark observables need to be mass-dependent and flavor-independent. While the nominal top quark mass is a well-established parameter, further investigation is required to ensure its flavor invariance. Following an explanation of the significance of the top quark mass in various models and its measurement process, the properties of the nominal top quark mass as an effective parameter are examined, with a discussion on its inherent flavor invariance based on perturbative and non-perturbative factors. While the nominal top quark mass has inherent properties that reduce its flavor dependence to a negligible level, further study is required to fully establish its flavor invariance at a phenomenological level, with a particular focus on its non-perturbative components.

An edge-tinting on a graph G involves assigning a color to each edge, 
with the condition that each vertex maintains a specific color count from 
red through to red and additional red dots. A 2-edge-tinting, for example, 
allows a vertex to show any combination of red and blue colors. Researchers 
have investigated the minimum number of colors required for 2-edge-tinting 
in subgraphs of certain types of nearly regular graphs, specifically K_2m 
y graphs and grid graphs of size r by s. By achieving some of these results 
indirectly, new upper limits for 2-edge-tinting in grid graphs are also 
determined.

We establish a generalised version of the hypercontractive inequality for functions in certain modified versions of the Bergman space. In addition, we identify specific parameters for these modified spaces where the hypercontractive inequality becomes ineffective. Our proof relies on the association of the Bergman space with the space of analytic functions defined on a specific subset of the complex plane with a particular measure. We consider a conformal mapping of this subset and introduce the Radon-Nikodym derivative for the transformed measure. Our approach enables us to extend a previous finding from Pavlov and Seip, which concerned the Bargmann-Fock space, to our modified Bergman spaces. We also provide alternative, more straightforward calculations that were missing in Pavlov and Seip's work.

The early identification of COVID-19 via computed tomography (CT) images is critical in combating the pandemic and preventing the overwhelming of the healthcare system. Despite advancements, accurately detecting COVID-19 from conventional dose CT scans and distinguishing it from non-infectious pulmonary diseases remains a significant challenge. Researchers have primarily used 3D convolutional neural networks (CNNs) for image-based COVID--19 detection, but these networks can struggle with transferring knowledge to other datasets due to issues with hyperparameter overfitting. Moreover, pre-trained 3D CNNs often require significant computational resources and can be inefficient when processing large images. To overcome these limitations, we developed a two-stage, time-distributed capsule network (TCN) that can detect COVID-19 from low-dose CT scans with high accuracy. The network consists of two main modules. The first module uses axial-slice TCN, comprising a 3D convolutional layer and a temporal-distributed layer derived from a dynamic UNet, to capture detailed features at the slice level. The second module employs reconstructed reconstructions with the axial-slice TCN and incorporates transverse capsule dynamic layers to aggregate features from different slices and identify the disease's focus and intensity. We evaluated our TCN network on a publicly available dataset and found that it outperformed existing COVID-19 detection methods, with an overall accuracy of 93.37% (+8.16% vs. 3D dynamic UNet, the best-performing baseline

In the highly crowded low-Earth orbit region, accurately estimating the available space around an object has become a pressing concern. This importance is further amplified by the upcoming proliferation of small satellites, which will only serve to complicate mission operations. We present a method to estimate the available space around a moving object of a standard specification in low-Earth orbit by accounting for the objects' spatial boundaries and gravitational pull of major celestial bodies. This method utilizes elliptical orbits with periodic changes in altitude, velocity, and position, which are accurately accounted for in the algorithm. The algorithm's accuracy has been verified for objects in six distinct types of orbits, confirming it as a useful tool for mission operators.

Recent advances in mesh optimization have significantly improved mesh quality, but many existing methods focus on removing irregular elements while allowing irregular ones first. In contrast, we introduce an innovative, high-order quadrilateral mesh creation approach from CAD models that directly optimizes for high-quality elements using an entire optimization matrix. By transforming mesh constraints into linear optimization problems with no limitations on element types, our method efficiently produces high-quality meshes with fewer, more regular elements. Distinguishing it from standard approaches, our novel optimization matrix introduces new variables to ensure mesh validity, but omits variables that would otherwise result in bad elements. Furthermore, we have developed and incorporated constraints that prevent mesh collapse and ensure mesh integrity during the optimization process. We demonstrate through a series of numerical experiments that our method effectively produces high-order meshes with minimal elements and optimal quality.

Correlation analysis is a widely used tool in data analysis for identifying linear relationships within datasets. To gauge the significance of observed correlations, statistical tests must be conducted, which often necessitate complex computational procedures. To streamline this process, this research develops a mathematical framework to quickly calculate correlation metrics on any data configuration. Leveraging this new formalism, developers can easily create data analysis algorithms, including those optimized for parallel processing. To facilitate practical application of these findings, this study also introduces a correlation metric based on the average correlation within all data subsets, along with associated formulas for computing mean correlation. Additionally, formulas for estimating standard error and z-scores are provided, allowing users to directly apply these formulas in correlation analysis without needing to derive them herself.

We detail the process for utilizing the general scattering theory framework known as Generalised Algebraic Structure for Scattering Matrices (GASSMAT), and its implementation in Mathematica. The provided code enables the evaluation of GASSMAT to verify the discovery of a previously unused dimension in the Universe, confirming the presence of 3 spatial and 1 temporal dimensions, and yielding Einstein's theory of General Relativity as a potential outcome of the theory. Einstein's theory of General Relativity can be derived as a limiting case of GASSMAT, validating the first postulate of special relativity and revealing a unified theory that encompasses both quantum mechanics and General Relativity.

abla \cdot \omega \otimes x + \mathbf{n} \cdot 
abla \omega + \mathbf{f})$ within $L^3$-like spaces in a bounded domain. By leveraging a novel computational approach, we demonstrate that the NS systems can be stabilized with low-dimensional feedback from within. Specifically, we utilize computational methods to derive sharp estimates for the high-frequency energy of a generalized model, which takes the form $\mathbf{v}_t - \Delta \mathbf{v} = (
abla \cdot \mathbf{v} \otimes x + \mathbf{f} + \mathbf{h})$. Building on this, we show that the Navier-Stokes equations, defined as $\omega_t - \Delta \omega = (
abla \cdot \omega \otimes x + \mathbf{n} \cdot 
abla \omega + \mathbf{f})$ within $L^3$-like spaces in a bounded domain, can be stabilized with low-dimensional feedback from within. Specifically, we show that the NS systems can be stabilized with 4-dimensional feedback from within when $\mathbf{f} = 0$, and that the dimension increases to 7 when $\mathbf{f} 
eq 0$.

Language learning is significantly benefited by a comprehensive dictionary that covers a broad range of words. Although there are numerous dictionaries accessible through the internet, word coverage and scope may vary, and may not always align with the needs of language learners or users. To address this, a decision was made to create a user-friendly online dictionary that could be customized for language learning purposes. The resulting dictionary, known as LitMind Lexicon, is a practical resource that is not only easily accessible from anywhere but also open-source and adaptable to different users' needs. The dictionary's user-friendly design enables quick searching of words using a variety of input methods, including typing a few characters, speaking, or pasting text. The dictionary's open-source nature also allows for collaborative modification, and it can be easily integrated into third-party platforms like MindLexicon, a comprehensive vocabulary database containing over 250,000 English words and definitions collected over 15 years.

To build trust in recommended items, users need to understand how and why they were suggested. Interpretability techniques aim to provide this understanding by increasing transparency in complex systems. Recent advances have offered increased scrutiny for machine learning models, but existing work primarily focuses on text-based explanations. This research explores the potential of saliability in visual data explanations through the use of saliency maps from Light Gradient Explainable, an efficient and lightweight method. We evaluate this approach in a real-world scenario with movie ratings and find that users prefer explanations generated by this method, which also meets the desired stability and compliance requirements for practical use in recommendation systems.

The x-ray valence photoemission spectroscopy (XVPS) analysis allowed us to accurately measure the energy level of the conduction band with respect to the Fermi level. The XVPS technique also facilitated the accurate alignment of the energy levels in relation to the near-surface region. The results showed that the energy level of the energy confinement in the quantum wells with 7 and 10 monolayers of InAs shifted towards the valence band in contrast to the calculation which indicated a shift towards the conduction band in comparison to unstrained materials. Designing machine learning systems that withstand uncertainty and changes is crucial, as real-world data often changes over time. While quantification of model robustness under data shift has become possible, the impact of data distribution changes on models trained with different data subsets remains poorly understood. In particular, the effect of using regional queries on learning outcomes remains a mystery. This study fills this knowledge gap by examining how training with regional queries affects model performance. Our investigation involved analyzing three datasets, which we replicated and extended to investigate the techniques used by regional query methods. Our findings show that regional queries can either harm or improve model performance, depending on various factors, such as the time of query sampling and the distinctness of the dataset subsets. This research also introduces new metrics to assess the potential benefits and drawbacks of using regional queries for learning, providing a comprehensive understanding of this approach's impact.

Our previous research successfully reduced the time complexity of Sinkhorn iterations from $O(N^3)$ to $O(N)$, and this study takes it a step further, achieving a fully iterative termination process with a single band matrix inversion per iteration. This advancement is made possible by introducing the concept of the collinear triangular array (CTA), allowing for quick and efficient generation of a Sinkhorn matrix. Additionally, we propose the concept of precise projection (PP), a computationally efficient method to approximate the optimal transport plan within a margin of error. By leveraging the properties of CTA, PP can be realized in $O(N)$ time. This research showcases that with sufficient iterations, the Sinkhorn iterations can converge, and an optimal solution can be obtained with a time complexity determined solely by the row-per-row projection (RPR) operation. Under the assumption of PP, an exact solution to the optimal transport problem can be obtained in $O(N)$ time by leveraging the properties of CTA. This research takes a step towards demystifying the optimal transport solution by providing an analytical expression of the optimal transport plan. This solution can be obtained in $O(N)$ time.

AU Mic is a young star closely surrounded by two planets that are heavily influenced by its strong stellar radiation. Detecting the star's emissions in the far ultraviolet (FUV) has shown that it has a broad spectrum of white light that is not seen in the near ultraviolet (NUV). Emissions in the FUV are typically seen in young stars but not in mid-to-late spectral type stars. AU Mic's radiation in the FUV is thought to be a result of its interaction with its surrounding planetary material, specifically its impact on its stellar magnetic field. This effect, known as the Rayleigh-Taylor instability, causes stars to emit UV radiation. Observations of AU Mic in both quiescent and eruptive states have shown that its radiation in the FUV increases during star eruptions. This increase in the radiation is also seen in the star's fast-moving stellar winds, which are thought to be a result of its planetary activity. AU Mic's b is believed to be in a habitable zone, whereas AU Mic c is in a region with high stellar radiation. During star eruptions, this radiation increases further, potentially making c an unlikely candidate for supporting life.

When high-speed charged particles interact with dense matter, it slows down due to a static drag effect. This interaction also generates an electrical resistance, which is influenced by the drag effect. The drag effect's magnitude can be determined by evaluating the slow-down of the particles, using concepts from classical physics. On the other hand, the electrical resistance can be understood by considering the drag effect's impact using the principles of Fermi liquids. This study explores the drag effect's broader applicability to electronic Fermi liquids and illustrates that the drag effect in such systems is associated with the density of states at the Fermi level. A universal drag coefficient is derived, which does not rely on specific models but rather the Landau parameters. By generalizing the Luttinger ansatz, we demonstrate that the drag effect is connected to the difference between the density of states at the Fermi level in the moving and stationary states. Additionally, we identify a correlation between the drag effect and the emission of Cerenkov radiation, which depends on the drag effect's magnitude. The drag effect's predictions are compared with existing data from high-energy particle physics and penetrating cosmic rays, showing promising results. The study also discusses the drag effect's potential applications and challenges in future high-speed particle research.

When the training database comprising the features of future class-A1 samples does not include any class-A2 data, we develop an method to make class-A2 predictions based on the training data that is available. Given the inherent asymmetry in the problem, we propose a classification approach tailored to these uneven conditions. From a statistical perspective, we demonstrate that the proposed method produces an accurate estimator for the probability that a given sample belongs to class-A2. This estimator's reliability is established through both the central limit theorem and a convergent sequence of functions. Lastly, simulations revealing the error rates of the method are also conducted and discussed.
